analysis.one_liner: Requires large social media platforms to share data with vetted researchers and publicly disclose ads, algorithms, and moderation.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six senators from both parties, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2023 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force large social media platforms to hand data to approved university and nonprofit researchers so they can independently study how these services affect society. It would also require platforms to publish searchable public records of their advertisements, widely-seen content, content moderation decisions, and how their recommendation algorithms work. The Federal Trade Commission and National Science Foundation would run the program and set privacy safeguards, and platforms that refused to cooperate could be sued or enforced against.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be the public and independent researchers. Researchers at U.S. universities and nonprofits would gain a legal, protected way to get data from platforms with 50 million or more U.S. users, instead of depending on the platforms' goodwill. Ordinary users would get to see who paid for the ads targeting them, what content was amplified or suppressed, how content moderation actually works, and how the algorithms decide what they see. Journalists and researchers doing public-interest investigations would get protection from lawsuits for collecting public platform data.

how_it_helps.text: Gives vetted university and nonprofit researchers a legally protected pathway to data held by platforms with at least 50 million U.S. monthly users, with the NSF approving projects on scientific merit and the FTC setting privacy and cybersecurity safeguards for the data.
Excludes the most sensitive data from researcher access: direct private messages, biometric information like fingerprints and voiceprints, and precise location data.

Requires platforms to publish searchable public repositories of advertising — who paid, who was targeted and why, how many people were reached, and whether algorithms amplified or restricted the ad — plus a repository of highly disseminated content (viewed by at least 10,000 unique users) and content from major public accounts.

Requires platforms to report publicly, at least twice a year, on how their recommendation and ranking algorithms work — what signals they use, what they optimize for — and to publish statistics on content moderation, including how much violating content was viewed and how it was identified.

Protects news-gathering and public-interest research — including scraping public pages, using research accounts, and collecting data users consent to donate — from civil and criminal liability through an FTC-issued safe harbor.

Gives researchers a real enforcement tool: if a platform refuses to provide required data, the researcher or their institution can sue in federal court or ask the FTC to act, and the platform may not cut off an ongoing project's data access without notifying the FTC.

analysis.who_pays: Large social media platforms (companies like Meta, TikTok, X, and YouTube) would bear the costs: building secure systems to deliver data to researchers, disclosing advertising and targeting details they currently keep private, explaining their algorithms publicly, and publishing detailed moderation statistics. They would also lose control over the gatekeeping power that comes from deciding who gets to study their data. Some compliance costs could ultimately show up in the platforms' operations, but the direct cost falls on the companies.

drawbacks.text: Moving platform user data to outside researchers creates real privacy risk. The bill addresses this with FTC-mandated safeguards (encryption, de-identification, access logs) and by barring researchers from re-identifying individuals or sharing data with third parties, and it excludes private messages, biometrics, and precise location — but any expansion of data access carries breach risk that did not exist before.

The bill concentrates significant gatekeeping power in federal agencies: every research finding must pass FTC prepublication review before release, and decisions about which research projects are approved cannot be challenged in court. Critics of any administration could reasonably worry about who controls which studies see the light of day.

Platforms would face substantial compliance costs and risk of exposing trade secrets through the mandated transparency reporting; the bill directs the FTC to protect trade secrets and user privacy and lets it reduce disclosure requirements if platforms face manipulation risks, but the burden on the companies would be real.

Researchers would be limited to U.S. universities and nonprofits, and platforms would get the right to comment on and appeal research project approvals — provisions that could slow or narrow the research the bill is meant to enable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gain here is transparency into services that shape what hundreds of millions of Americans see and read — who is paying to reach them, what gets amplified, and how the algorithms work — which today is known almost entirely to the platforms themselves. The privacy and security risks are genuine but the bill takes them seriously, with mandatory safeguards, excluded categories of data, and criminal and civil penalties for researchers who violate the rules. The most legitimate concern is not privacy but agency power: FTC prepublication review of findings and no judicial review of approvals give the government real control over platform research. On balance, this is a carefully designed bill whose benefits to the public would likely outweigh its costs, though it is not flawless.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took it up after referring the bill, so it sat untouched until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Coons introduced the bill on June 8, 2023 with five cosponsors split across both parties: Democrats Amy Klobuchar and Richard Blumenthal and Republicans Bill Cassidy, John Cornyn, and Mitt Romney.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That was the last action ever taken. The committee held no hearing, no markup, and never voted on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media platforms are better off: they keep sole control of their data, their ad-targeting details, and their algorithm information, and face no new transparency obligations or litigation risk from researchers. Users and researchers are exactly where they were.

for.name: Sen. Chris Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Platform Accountability and Transparency Act on June 8, 2023.

for.name: Bipartisan group of five Senate cosponsors (Blumenthal, Klobuchar — D; Cassidy, Cornyn, Romney — R)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill support from both parties at introduction.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Her committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; the record shows no action beyond the June 8, 2023 referral.

against.name: Large social media platforms
against.what_they_did: Would have faced mandated data sharing, public ad and algorithm disclosures, and litigation risk from researchers; industry resistance to such data-access mandates is widely reported, though it does not appear in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan from day one, with three Republicans and two Democrats cosponsoring the Democratic sponsor's bill.

industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. users would have been required to hand data to approved researchers, publish public repositories of ads and viral content, explain their algorithms, and disclose moderation statistics — giving up control of information that currently only they can see. Because the bill died in committee, they gave up nothing and keep their gatekeeping role over who studies them.

The bill would have forced public disclosure of who pays for ads, the targeting and exclusion parameters used, and how many people each ad reached — exposing ad targeting practices that today are visible mainly to the platforms and the advertisers themselves. This is one of the bill's direct transparency benefits to the public.

Academic and nonprofit researchers would have gained guaranteed, legally protected access to platform data, plus immunity for public-interest data collection like scraping and research accounts. Their gain is the public's gain, since their findings are how the public learns what platforms are doing.
